statement: PDAC arises in the exocrine tissue that makes up most of the pancreas.
A KRAS mutation is the initiating genetic change in nearly every PDAC.
Microscopic PanIN lesions are the precursors from which most PDAC develops.
Most PDACs arise in the head of the pancreas, where they block the bile duct early and are found sooner than body or tail tumors.
A PDAC tumor contains a dense scar-like stroma that often outweighs the cancer cells themselves.
PDAC is the most common and most aggressive of several distinct pancreatic tumor types.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet-type hormone-producing cells, not from the duct cells that give rise to PDAC.
Acinar cell carcinoma arises from the enzyme-making acinar cells and follows a different course from PDAC.
An IPMN or mucinous cystic neoplasm can, over years, give rise to an invasive adenocarcinoma, though most never do.
Cancers of the ampulla and lower bile duct sit beside the pancreatic head and are grouped with PDAC as periampullary cancers.
Adenosquamous and body-tail tumors are enriched for the squamous molecular state that marks the more aggressive end of PDAC.
PDAC is the ductal adenocarcinoma that the other pancreatic tumor types are compared against.
Resectability categories are a separate axis from TNM stage and are decided from vessel contact on CT.
The number of cancer-containing lymph nodes is the component of stage that most strongly separates survival after resection.
The pathological stage, grade and margin status are read from the resected specimen described in the pathology report.
The degree of tumor-vessel contact on CT determines resectability, independently of the tumor's stage.
A resectable tumor of the pancreatic head is removed by a Whipple operation if the patient is fit enough to undergo it.
Contact with the superior mesenteric and portal veins is the main criterion separating resectable from borderline resectable disease.
Encasement of the superior mesenteric artery is what makes a tumor locally advanced rather than borderline.
Resectability categories are assigned from the degree of tumor-vessel contact reported on pancreas-protocol CT.
Borderline resectable and locally advanced categories are the settings in which chemotherapy before surgery is standard.
Restaging after chemotherapy often leaves a tumor in the same category even when it has become removable.
Borderline resectable tumors touching the vein are often removed with a planned vein resection and reconstruction.
Restaging scans after chemotherapy are the commonest trigger for a change of plan, and they are also where CT is least reliable.
A staging laparoscopy that finds hidden spread converts a surgical plan into a systemic-therapy plan.
Germline and tumor sequencing results that arrive weeks after diagnosis can add a targeted drug to the plan.
A CA 19-9 trend, read after bile-duct drainage, is one of the measurements a tumor board uses to revise a plan.
A second opinion at a high-volume center can move a tumor from one resectability category to another.
Chemotherapy before surgery is partly a test of tumor behavior whose result can change the surgical plan.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is one of the sequencing choices among chemotherapy before, after or instead of surgery.
Modified FOLFIRINOX is the regimen most often given before surgery for borderline resectable pancreatic cancer.
Whether chemotherapy comes first depends on the resectability category assigned at diagnosis.
Chemotherapy before surgery is aimed at the microscopic disease that is usually present at diagnosis.
Adding radiation to preoperative chemotherapy for borderline disease did not improve outcomes in a randomized trial.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is followed by restaging scans that decide whether surgery goes ahead.
Minimal residual disease after surgery is detected, imperfectly, by circulating tumor DNA tests.
The liver is prepared in advance to receive disseminated pancreatic cancer cells by tumor-derived signals.
Microscopic disease left after treatment is the source of later recurrence.
A clear scan cannot exclude microscopic disease, which lies below imaging resolution.
Adjuvant and neoadjuvant chemotherapy are given to treat microscopic disease that no scan can show.
The liver is the commonest site where microscopic pancreatic cancer deposits later grow into visible metastases.
A clear or stable scan is the main output of restaging after treatment, and its limits are those of CT.
A CA 19-9 trend complements a clear scan but is uninformative in people who cannot make the marker.
Circulating tumor DNA can reveal recurrence months before a scan but misses about half of residual disease.
Staging laparoscopy finds hidden spread in about one in six patients whose scans appear clear of metastases.
A clear scan says nothing about microscopic disease, which lies below imaging resolution.
PET can distinguish metabolically active tumor from scar better than size on CT, though inflammation also lights up.
Recurrence grows from microscopic disease that was present but invisible at the time of the original treatment.
The liver is the commonest site of recurrence because tumor signals prepare it to receive disseminated cells.
Liver recurrence carries a shorter course than lung recurrence after pancreatic resection.
Rising circulating tumor DNA often signals recurrence months before a scan shows it.
Recurrent and metastatic clones descend from subclones of the original tumor that keep evolving in each organ.
Recurrence after surgery is treated with the systemic therapies used for metastatic disease.
Trial endpoints such as median survival and hazard ratios describe groups, and survival statistics explain why they do not forecast individuals.
The endpoints described here are what phase 2 and phase 3 clinical trials are built to measure.
Maintenance olaparib is the clearest pancreatic cancer example of progression-free survival improving without a significant overall survival gain.
Daraxonrasib's phase 3 trial improved response, progression-free survival and overall survival together, which is why it changed practice.
The hyaluronidase trial raised response rate without changing survival, a lesson about what response measures.
Reading endpoints correctly is the first step in judging whether a headline result counts as progress.
Daraxonrasib is the clearest pancreatic cancer example of a phase 1/2 signal confirmed by a randomized phase 3 and converted into approval.
The RASolute 302, 303 and 304 trials show the phase 3 program that follows an approved drug into new settings.
The personalized mRNA vaccine is a phase 1 result awaiting its randomized phase 2 readout.
Immune combination trials in pancreatic cancer illustrate early signals that shrank toward no effect under randomization.
Judging a trial requires reading its endpoints as well as its phase.
What counts as progress depends on whether a result has survived a randomized comparison.
Pembrolizumab's tissue-agnostic approval shows how a drug can be labeled for pancreatic cancer on evidence mostly from other tumors.
The medians and hazard ratios in survival statistics are the same quantities that trial results report.
Stage-specific survival figures depend on nodal status, which is why stage and resectability must be read separately.
Survival figures from patients resected after neoadjuvant therapy describe a selected group and overstate what everyone who starts can expect.
Trial survival figures apply to the fit, selected patients who met the trial's eligibility rules.
A CA 19-9 trend is one of the individual features that moves a person within the group a survival statistic describes.
A tumor in the head of the pancreas is the usual cause of jaundice because the common bile duct passes through the head.
Jaundice signals that the common bile duct is blocked before it reaches the ampulla in the duodenum.
Jaundice from a blocked bile duct is usually relieved by a metal biliary stent placed during ERCP.
The Whipple operation removes the head of the pancreas and the lower bile duct, relieving jaundice permanently when the tumor can be resected.
Fever with returning jaundice signals cholangitis, an infection of the blocked bile duct that needs urgent drainage.
Bile-duct obstruction inflates CA 19-9, so the marker is interpreted after jaundice has been drained.
Pain from pancreatic cancer travels through the celiac plexus, the nerve web that can be blocked to relieve it.
Nerves remodeled inside the tumor, with their Schwann cells and surrounding mast cells, are a proposed cause of pancreatic cancer pain.
The same tumor signal, GDF15, is implicated in both pancreatic cancer pain and cachexia.
Part of pancreatic pain is relieved by enzyme replacement because undigested food distends the gut.
Pain in pancreatic cancer is managed by palliative-care teams alongside oncology treatment.
A sudden change in pain with fever or vomiting can mean cholangitis or a blockage rather than tumor pain.
Enzyme insufficiency is the gut-side cause of weight loss in pancreatic cancer and responds to enzyme replacement.
Cachexia in pancreatic cancer is treated with counseling, appetite medicines and investigational GDF-15 blockade.
The phase 3 ponsegromab trial tests whether blocking GDF-15 reverses cachexia in pancreatic cancer.
Weight loss in pancreatic cancer is addressed first through dietitian-led nutrition and protein intake.
Muscle loss in cachexia limits physical function even though strength can improve with training.
GDF-15, the cytokine driving cachexia, also promotes pain through Schwann cells in pancreatic cancer.
Enzyme insufficiency follows loss or obstruction of the acinar cells that make pancreatic digestive enzymes.
A tumor blocking the main pancreatic duct prevents enzymes from reaching the intestine and causes insufficiency.
Exocrine insufficiency is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement capsules taken with every meal.
After a Whipple, enzyme insufficiency persists in most people because the rebuilt anatomy mistimes enzyme and food delivery.
Undigested fat and protein from enzyme insufficiency is one of the two engines of weight loss in pancreatic cancer.
Enzyme replacement is the precondition for nutrition advice to work when fat is passing through undigested.
Cancer-associated diabetes arises from suppressed islet function, while surgical diabetes arises from loss of islet mass.
Diabetes after pancreatic surgery is managed with monitoring and insulin as described under managing blood sugar after surgery.
Total pancreatectomy causes immediate insulin-requiring diabetes in every patient.
New-onset diabetes with weight loss is a risk marker for pancreatic cancer rather than a screening test.
Rising blood sugar precedes the fat and muscle loss of pancreatic cancer by about a year.
Dexamethasone given to prevent chemotherapy nausea raises blood sugar for a day or two each cycle.
The cytokine signaling that drives cachexia also lowers activity and contributes to fatigue in pancreatic cancer.
Fatigue is partly countered by light regular activity, which improved walking capacity during treatment.
Depression and poor sleep are common contributors to fatigue in pancreatic cancer and are treatable.
Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel caused severe fatigue in 17% of patients, more than gemcitabine alone.
Undigested food from enzyme insufficiency drains energy and is a treatable contributor to fatigue.
Palliative-care teams address the symptom cluster of fatigue, pain, sleep and appetite together.
Irinotecan causes both an early cholinergic diarrhea and a late diarrhea from damage to the intestinal lining.
FOLFIRINOX causes diarrhea in roughly a quarter of patients at severe grade and nausea that standard prevention controls in most.
Inherited UGT1A1 and DPYD variants raise the risk of severe diarrhea and low blood counts from irinotecan and fluorouracil.
Greasy floating stools during chemotherapy are usually enzyme insufficiency rather than drug diarrhea.
Vomiting of food eaten hours earlier signals a blocked duodenum rather than chemotherapy nausea.
Dexamethasone used to prevent chemotherapy nausea raises blood sugar for a day or two each cycle.
Oxaliplatin causes both the acute cold-triggered tingling and the cumulative numbness of chemotherapy neuropathy.
FOLFIRINOX produces neuropathy through its oxaliplatin component, which is often stopped early to limit it.
Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel causes a cumulative sensory neuropathy in about 17% at severe grade.
NALIRIFOX caused less neuropathy than gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel in a head-to-head trial.
Chemotherapy neuropathy in the hands and feet is distinct from tumor-related nerve pain in the abdomen and back.
Dose reductions and delays, the main protection against neuropathy, are part of the same dose-adjustment decisions described with growth-factor support.
Febrile neutropenia risk with FOLFIRINOX is reduced with growth-factor injections and dose adjustments.
Inherited UGT1A1 and DPYD variants raise the risk of severe neutropenia from irinotecan and fluorouracil.
FOLFIRINOX is classed as a high-risk regimen for febrile neutropenia, which affected 20% of patients in one cohort.
A biliary stent can become a source of bloodstream infection when neutrophils are low.
Fever with jaundice during chemotherapy points to cholangitis in a blocked or stented bile duct.
Fever with new or returning jaundice is the warning sign of cholangitis described under jaundice.
Clots in pancreatic cancer are prevented and treated with anticoagulants as described under preventing and treating blood clots.
A tumor pressing on the portal or superior mesenteric vein can cause visceral vein thrombosis.
Dehydration from chemotherapy diarrhea or vomiting raises clot risk in pancreatic cancer.
Clot risk in pancreatic cancer is higher with metastatic disease.
Stent exchanges and other procedures require anticoagulation to be paused and restarted on a schedule.
Gastric outlet obstruction occurs when a pancreatic head tumor narrows the duodenum that wraps around it.
Bile-duct blockage and cholangitis arise where the common bile duct passes through the pancreatic head to the ampulla.
A blocked bile duct is treated with a metal biliary stent, which itself can block or become infected.
Returning jaundice after a stent is the first sign that the stent has blocked.
Tumors in the head of the pancreas cause almost all bile-duct and duodenal blockages.
Cancer deposits on the peritoneum are the usual cause of bowel obstruction in pancreatic cancer.
Fever with a blocked or stented bile duct is cholangitis and is managed as an infection emergency.
Nutrition slows the weight loss of pancreatic cancer cachexia but cannot by itself reverse its systemic drive.
Nutrition advice in pancreatic cancer depends on enzyme replacement to make eaten fat and protein absorbable.
Enzyme capsules taken with every meal are the first step in nutrition through pancreatic cancer treatment.
Appetite medicines and investigational GDF-15 blockade address the part of weight loss that nutrition cannot.
Protein intake and activity together preserve the muscle and function needed to tolerate treatment.
Persistent vomiting of old food is a blocked stomach outlet rather than a nutrition problem.
Cachexia limits muscle mass even when training improves strength and function.
Physical function, scored as performance status, is one of the fitness questions that decides which treatments are offered.
Light regular activity was associated with less fatigue and improved walking capacity during treatment.
Exercise was associated with more open blood vessels inside resected tumors, an experimental finding.
Preoperative exercise was associated with more CD8 T cells inside tumors, an experimental finding.
The months of chemotherapy before surgery are the window in which prehabilitation is offered.
Distress and depression in pancreatic cancer are addressed by palliative-care teams that include psychological support.
Depression and poor sleep are common contributors to fatigue in pancreatic cancer.
Pain distress and psychological distress travel together in pancreatic cancer and each worsens the other.
Survival statistics are a major source of distress and are best read with someone who can explain which group a number describes.
Changes of treatment plan are predictable moments of distress for patients and families.
Palliative-care teams manage pancreatic cancer pain with medicines, nerve blocks and enzyme replacement.
Palliative care includes distress screening and psychological support for patients and caregivers.
Palliative-care teams coordinate the nutrition, enzyme and appetite measures used for cachexia.
Palliative-care teams help detect and manage the clots that are common in pancreatic cancer.
Palliative-care teams coordinate stents and bypasses for bile-duct and duodenal blockages.
Palliative-care teams help people weigh options when a treatment plan changes.
Life after a Whipple follows from what the Whipple operation removes and rebuilds.
Fistula, delayed gastric emptying and bleeding are the early complications that shape the first weeks after a Whipple.
Enzyme insufficiency after a Whipple persists in most people because the rebuilt anatomy mistimes enzyme and food delivery.
Digestion after a Whipple is supported by enzyme replacement capsules taken with every meal.
New diabetes after a Whipple or pancreatectomy is managed as described under managing blood sugar after surgery.
Total pancreatectomy replaces the partial-resection picture with immediate insulin-dependent diabetes.
Weight and strength after a Whipple are supported by protein-first eating and dietitian follow-up.
Surveillance after a Whipple continues because recurrence remains the main risk after resection.
The pancreas includes the head and uncinate process, which sit in the curve of the duodenum.
The pancreas includes the neck, the thin segment that crosses in front of the superior mesenteric and portal veins.
The pancreas includes the body and tail, which cross the aorta and reach the spleen.
The pancreas is drained along its full length by the main pancreatic duct.
The pancreas is mostly made of acinar cells, which manufacture digestive enzymes.
The pancreas's duct cells line the duct tree and secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.
The pancreas contains the islets of Langerhans, which release insulin and glucagon.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma arises within the pancreas, most often in the head.
The pancreas also gives rise to neuroendocrine tumors and acinar cell carcinoma, which are distinct from PDAC.
The head and uncinate process form the right-hand, widest part of the pancreas.
The lower common bile duct runs down through the back of the pancreatic head to the ampulla.
The duodenum cradles the pancreatic head and shares its blood supply, so the two are removed together.
The uncinate process of the head hooks behind the superior mesenteric vein.
The uncinate process reaches toward the superior mesenteric artery, which lies behind the vein.
Lymph from the head drains to stations in front of and behind the head and along the superior mesenteric artery.
Nerves reach the uncinate process from the superior mesenteric plexus along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.
A head tumor is removed by the Whipple operation, which takes the head, duodenum and lower bile duct as one block.
A tumor in the pancreatic head blocks the bile duct and causes jaundice.
The neck is the thin segment of the pancreas between the head and the body.
The neck of the pancreas crosses directly in front of the superior mesenteric vein–portal vein confluence.
Tumors of the neck are often classified as borderline resectable because of their contact with the vein behind them.
Contact between a neck tumor and the vein is measured on pancreas-protocol CT as degrees of circumference.
A neck tumor involving the vein is removed together with a segment of the vein, which is then reconstructed.
The neck is where the pancreas is divided, and a soft gland with a small duct here is the main risk factor for a pancreatic fistula.
The body and tail form the left half of the pancreas, from the neck to the spleen.
The tail of the pancreas reaches the hilum of the spleen, which is removed with the tail in cancer surgery.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the body and tail and the splenic vein runs along their back.
The body of the pancreas lies directly on the celiac plexus, which supplies its nerves and carries its pain signals.
A tumor of the body or tail is removed by distal pancreatectomy together with the spleen.
Body and tail tumors typically present with back pain rather than jaundice.
Body and tail tumors are more likely than head tumors to have hidden peritoneal spread found at laparoscopy.
Body and tail tumors are often staged by laparoscopy because of their higher rate of imaging-invisible spread.
The main pancreatic duct runs the full length of the pancreas from tail to head.
The pancreatic duct is lined by duct cells that secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.
The pancreatic duct and the common bile duct run side by side through the head and share an opening at the ampulla.
Dilatation or abrupt cutoff of the pancreatic duct on CT is an indirect sign of a tumor that may itself be invisible.
MRI can display the pancreatic duct in detail without contrast, showing dilatation and the level of obstruction.
Obstruction of the pancreatic duct by a tumor cuts off enzyme delivery and causes maldigestion.
IPMN cysts arise within the pancreatic duct system and are a separate, slower precursor pathway.
PanIN precursor lesions arise in the small branches of the pancreatic duct tree.
Acinar cells make up most of the tissue of the pancreas.
In mouse models, acinar cells are the main cell of origin of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
Acinar cells reprogrammed into a duct-like state give rise to PanIN precursor lesions.
Loss of acinar enzyme delivery to the gut causes the exocrine insufficiency common in pancreatic cancer.
The enzymes acinar cells no longer deliver can be replaced with capsules taken at meals.
Acinar cells deliver enzymes into channels lined by duct cells, which add bicarbonate and water.
A KRAS mutation in an acinar cell is the usual first step toward a PanIN lesion in mouse models.
Duct cells form the lining of the pancreatic duct tree.
Duct cells and acinar cells are controlled by different hormones, secretin and cholecystokinin respectively.
Duct cells can give rise to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by a route that skips low-grade PanIN.
PanIN precursor lesions form within the small ducts lined by duct cells.
The classical molecular subtype of PDAC most resembles normal duct cells.
Activating mutant Kras in duct cells produces few PanIN lesions in mice compared with acinar cells.
Islets are the endocrine component scattered through the pancreas.
Suppression of islet insulin release by the tumor causes the new-onset diabetes that often precedes a pancreatic cancer diagnosis.
Islets are about twice as dense in the tail as in the head or body.
The pancreatic polypeptide cells of the islets are concentrated in the uncinate process of the head.
Loss of islets at pancreatic surgery leads to diabetes that is managed with monitoring and, after total pancreatectomy, insulin.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet-type cells and are a different disease from PDAC.
The lower common bile duct runs through the back of the pancreatic head to the ampulla.
Blockage of the bile duct by a head tumor causes jaundice and itching.
A blocked bile duct is reopened with a stent placed endoscopically through the ampulla.
The bile duct carries bile from the liver, and its blockage raises liver enzyme tests and bilirubin.
Bile duct obstruction inflates CA 19-9, so the marker is interpreted after bilirubin falls.
The bile duct opens into the second part of the duodenum at the ampulla.
Fever with jaundice or a biliary stent is a warning sign of cholangitis in a blocked bile duct.
The bile duct and pancreatic duct run side by side through the head and share an opening at the ampulla.
The duodenum cradles the head of the pancreas and shares its blood supply.
The bile duct and pancreatic duct open into the second part of the duodenum at the ampulla.
The Whipple operation removes the duodenum together with the pancreatic head.
Narrowing of the duodenum by a head tumor causes gastric outlet obstruction with vomiting.
Head tumors are sampled by passing a needle through the duodenal wall under endoscopic ultrasound.
The duodenum receives food from the stomach through the pylorus.
Loss of the duodenum after a Whipple limits how well enzyme capsules mix with food.
The stomach lies directly in front of the body and tail of the pancreas across the lesser sac.
The stomach empties through the pylorus into the duodenum, which wraps around the pancreatic head.
A classic Whipple removes the antrum of the stomach, while the pylorus-preserving variant keeps it.
Delayed gastric emptying is a defined complication of pancreatic surgery affecting the stomach.
Body and tail tumors are sampled with a needle passed through the stomach wall under endoscopic ultrasound.
Blockage of the splenic vein by a body tumor reroutes blood through stomach-wall veins that can form varices.
A head tumor can block the stomach's outlet, causing vomiting and inability to eat.
The portal vein delivers blood from the pancreas to the liver, which is why the liver is the first site of spread.
The liver makes the bile that drains through the bile duct and pancreatic head to the duodenum.
The liver is prepared for metastasis by signals from the primary tumor before cancer cells arrive.
Small liver spots found on scans in pancreatic cancer may be metastases or benign and are characterized by MRI.
MRI detects small liver metastases better than CT and is used to characterize indeterminate liver lesions.
The liver is the commonest site of recurrence after pancreatic resection.
The hepatic artery supplies the liver and in about 16% of people has a variant course under the pancreatic head.
Bile backing up into the liver from a blocked duct causes jaundice and abnormal liver tests.
The tail of the pancreas reaches the hilum of the spleen.
The splenic artery and vein connect the spleen to the celiac axis and portal vein along the back of the pancreas.
The spleen is removed together with the body and tail in a distal pancreatectomy for cancer.
Clots in the splenic and portal veins are a recognized complication after splenectomy and in pancreatic cancer generally.
Removing the islet-rich tail with the spleen leads to diabetes in about 28% of people within a few years.
Lymph nodes draining the body and tail lie along the splenic artery and at the splenic hilum.
The neck of the pancreas crosses directly in front of the superior mesenteric vein–portal vein confluence.
The uncinate process of the pancreatic head hooks behind the superior mesenteric vein.
The portal vein carries blood from the pancreas to the liver, which is why the liver is the first site of metastasis.
Contact between a tumor and the superior mesenteric or portal vein is measured on CT in degrees of circumference.
Pancreas-protocol CT shows the relationship of the tumor to the superior mesenteric and portal veins.
An involved segment of the superior mesenteric or portal vein is removed with the tumor and reconstructed.
The degree of superior mesenteric or portal vein contact helps define resectable, borderline resectable and locally advanced disease.
After chemotherapy, scar at the vein interface looks like tumor on CT, so restaging scans over-call vein involvement.
Clots in the portal and mesenteric veins make up about a third of venous clots in pancreatic cancer.
The uncinate process of the pancreatic head hooks behind the vein toward the superior mesenteric artery.
The superior mesenteric artery runs behind and to the left of the superior mesenteric vein.
The superior mesenteric plexus wraps the artery and carries nerves to the uncinate process.
Lymph node station #14 surrounds the superior mesenteric artery and is involved in about a third of resected head cancers.
Contact between a tumor and the superior mesenteric artery is measured on CT in degrees of circumference.
The degree of superior mesenteric artery contact defines borderline resectable (up to 180 degrees) and locally advanced (more than 180 degrees) disease.
Tumors touching the superior mesenteric artery are usually treated with chemotherapy before any attempt at surgery.
The superior mesenteric artery arises just below the celiac axis and in about 12% of people gives off a replaced right hepatic artery.
The hepatic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreatic head, and a variant right hepatic artery passes beneath it.
The celiac axis supplies the liver through the common hepatic artery.
The celiac axis gives rise to the splenic artery, which runs along the pancreatic body and tail.
The celiac plexus surrounds the celiac axis and the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
Lymph node station #8 lies along the common hepatic artery and is involved in about 11% of resected head cancers.
Tumor contact with the celiac axis and hepatic artery is measured on CT in degrees of circumference.
Contact with the celiac axis or hepatic artery helps define borderline resectable and locally advanced disease.
Bleeding from the hepatic artery stump after a Whipple is a defined major complication.
The celiac axis arises from the aorta just above the superior mesenteric artery, and the two share the celiac plexus.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreatic body and tail and the splenic vein along their back.
The splenic artery and vein connect the spleen to the celiac axis and the portal vein.
The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac axis.
Blockage of the splenic vein reroutes blood through stomach-wall veins, which can form varices.
The splenic artery and vein are removed with the body, tail and spleen in a distal pancreatectomy for cancer.
The splenic vein is one of the abdominal veins in which cancer-related clots form.
Lymph from the pancreatic head drains to stations in front of and behind the head before reaching the superior mesenteric artery.
Lymph node station #14 surrounds the superior mesenteric artery and is the main route from the head toward the aorta.
Lymph node station #8 lies along the common hepatic artery.
Lymphatic and perineural spread from the uncinate process share the corridor along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.
Lymph node involvement is counted and reported as N stage in the pathology report after resection.
Lymph node involvement determines pathological stage but, apart from para-aortic nodes, does not by itself decide resectability.
A high lymph node ratio predicts recurrence within a year of surgery.
The Whipple operation removes the lymph node stations around the head and along the hepatic and superior mesenteric arteries.
The superior mesenteric plexus continues from the celiac plexus and wraps the superior mesenteric artery.
The celiac plexus surrounds the celiac axis and its branches.
The body and tail receive their nerves directly from the celiac plexus, which lies immediately above them.
The uncinate process receives nerves from the superior mesenteric plexus along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.
Pain signals from the pancreas travel through the celiac plexus and splanchnic nerves, and the plexus can be blocked to relieve pain.
Nerves inside the tumor are remodeled from the precancerous stage and influence both growth and pain.
Perineural invasion travels with lymph node spread and the two share routes along the arteries.
Perineural invasion is recorded in the pathology report after resection and predicts recurrence.
Peritoneal spread too small for scans is detected by staging laparoscopy with washings.
Body or tail location nearly tripled the odds of hidden peritoneal spread at laparoscopy compared with head tumors.
The peritoneum is one of the sites where microscopic disease invisible to scans persists.
A clear scan does not exclude peritoneal deposits, which were found at laparoscopy in 18% of imaging-localized cancers.
Peritoneal recurrence is one of the main patterns of distant failure after resection.
The peritoneum and the liver are the two main sites of hidden spread found at staging laparoscopy.
Tumor cells can rarely seed the needle track after endoscopic biopsy and later appear on the peritoneum.
Peritoneal deposits can kink or compress the bowel and cause intestinal blockage.
Desmoplasia is built by cancer-associated fibroblasts, which exist in several distinct states within the same tumor.
Desmoplasia includes the collagen and hyaluronan that generate the mechanical pressure measured inside pancreatic tumors.
Desmoplasia is proposed to compress the tumor's blood vessels, contributing to the poor perfusion and low oxygen found in pancreatic cancer.
Desmoplasia is the target of stroma-reprogramming strategies, which aim to change what the scar tissue does instead of removing it.
Desmoplasia is the subject of the stroma-targeting trials whose failures taught the field that less stroma is not the goal.
Desmoplasia shapes where T cells sit in a pancreatic tumor and how well they function once they arrive.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts are the cells that build the desmoplastic, scar-like stroma of a pancreatic tumor.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts secrete the collagen and hyaluronan whose swelling generates interstitial pressure inside the tumor.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts influence where T cells go in the tumor and how well they work once they reach the cancer cells.
Changes in cancer-associated fibroblasts are followed by changes in the macrophages and suppressive myeloid cells in the same tumor.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts are the intended target of stroma-reprogramming approaches, which aim to shift their state rather than delete them.
Cancer-associated fibroblast states sit alongside the cancer cells' own states as the two halves of what a tumor region is doing.
Matrix and the pressure it generates are the mechanical part of the desmoplastic reaction around a pancreatic tumor.
Matrix pressure is proposed to collapse the tumor's blood vessels, producing the poor perfusion and low oxygen seen in pancreatic cancer.
The amount of collagen and hyaluronan in the tumor is set by which cancer-associated fibroblast states are active.
The hyaluronan-degrading enzyme was tested as an addition to gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel, the regimen it was given alongside in the phase 3 trial.
Matrix-directed treatment is the clearest example of tumor shrinkage on scans without any gain in survival.
The hyaluronidase phase 3 shows why a response rate and a hazard ratio for death have to be read as separate results.
The pressure generated by matrix and hyaluronan is the proposed cause of the vessel collapse and poor perfusion in pancreatic tumors.
Poor blood supply and low oxygen are features of the tissue created by the desmoplastic reaction around a pancreatic cancer.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts both release vessel-growth signals and build the matrix that compresses vessels, so their state shapes the tumor's blood supply.
The same poor supply that starves a pancreatic tumor of oxygen leaves it short of glucose and glutamine, which is the setting for nutrient scavenging.
A tumor's poorer blood supply is what makes it enhance less than the surrounding pancreas on a contrast-enhanced CT scan.
Low oxygen in the tumor is one of the conditions that shapes the behavior of macrophages and other myeloid cells inside it.
The nutrient scarcity inside a pancreatic tumor follows from the poor, compressed blood supply and low oxygen described in the entry on blood supply and oxygen.
Mutant KRAS, the gene change covered in the KRAS entry, drives the fluid-gulping uptake route that supplies amino acids to pancreatic cancer cells.
Pancreatic stellate cells, the precursors of the cancer-associated fibroblast states described in that entry, feed alanine to pancreatic cancer cells through their own autophagy.
The same autophagy that feeds pancreatic cancer cells also carries their MHC class I molecules to the lysosome, which is the subject of the antigen presentation entry.
The hydroxychloroquine trials sit alongside the hyaluronidase trials in the entry on lessons from stroma-directed treatments, as the two clearest cases of tumor shrinkage without longer survival.

Activated stellate cells and fibroblasts carrying fibroblast activation protein (FAP), the cell states described in the cancer-associated fibroblasts entry, are the source of the CXCL12 that holds CD8 T cells away from pancreatic cancer cells.
Collagen density in the desmoplastic stroma did not reduce cytotoxic T-cell infiltration in resected human pancreatic tumors, so desmoplasia is not a simple wall keeping T cells out.

Irinotecan is one of the four drugs in FOLFIRINOX and the main source of its diarrhea and neutropenia.
Liposomal irinotecan is the irinotecan component of NALIRIFOX, the regimen approved first line in 2024.
Liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil and leucovorin is an approved second-line option after gemcitabine-based therapy.
Inherited UGT1A1 variants slow the clearance of irinotecan’s active metabolite and raise the risk of severe neutropenia.
Irinotecan-containing regimens carry a high risk of febrile neutropenia, which is why fever during treatment is an emergency.
Irinotecan causes an early cholinergic diarrhea and a late diarrhea from SN-38 released in the gut.
The neutropenia risk of irinotecan-containing FOLFIRINOX is one reason white-cell growth factors are considered from the first cycle.
Irinotecan and oxaliplatin are the two partner drugs that distinguish FOLFIRINOX from fluorouracil alone.
Liposomal irinotecan works only when combined with fluorouracil and leucovorin, not on its own.
Gemcitabine is one half of gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, where nab-paclitaxel raises the active form of gemcitabine inside tumor cells.
Gemcitabine was the comparator that FOLFIRINOX beat in metastatic disease and that modified FOLFIRINOX beat after surgery.
Gemcitabine replaced weekly bolus fluorouracil as the reference drug in 1997, and capecitabine was later added to gemcitabine after surgery.
Gemcitabine is the chemotherapy given alongside radiation in the PREOPANC chemoradiation schedule.
Gemcitabine's adjuvant trial against observation established the place of chemotherapy after surgery in treatment sequencing.
Gemcitabine-based first-line treatment precedes the second-line setting in which liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil and leucovorin was tested and approved.
Gemcitabine's effect is tracked by CA 19-9 in blood, where a 90% fall in the nab-paclitaxel trial marked longer survival.
Gemcitabine lowers neutrophils, so fever during treatment needs the urgent response described in the fever and infection topic.
The Whipple operation removes the head of the pancreas, where most pancreatic cancers arise.
The Whipple removes the duodenum because it shares its blood supply with the pancreatic head.
The Whipple removes the lower bile duct and ampulla, which pass through the pancreatic head.
The superior mesenteric and portal veins run behind the pancreatic neck and set the inner boundary of a Whipple.
The uncinate margin of a Whipple is dissected off the superior mesenteric artery, the usual site of a close margin.
Pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying and bleeding are the characteristic early complications of a Whipple.
The Whipple operation precedes the months of recovery and the permanent digestive changes described under life after a Whipple.
A Whipple may include resection and reconstruction of the portal or superior mesenteric vein when the tumor touches it.
The Whipple specimen is examined to report margins, lymph nodes and treatment response in the pathology report.
Whether a Whipple is offered up front or after chemotherapy depends on the resectability category assigned on imaging.
Jaundice before a Whipple may be relieved with a metal biliary stent when surgery is delayed for chemotherapy.
Digestion after a Whipple is supported by enzyme replacement capsules taken with every meal.
New diabetes after a Whipple depends more on body weight than on how much pancreas remains.
Distal pancreatectomy is the counterpart of the Whipple for tumors of the pancreatic body and tail.
A Whipple is extended to a total pancreatectomy when the tumor crosses the neck or the neck margin is positive.
Chemotherapy before or after a Whipple is part of every plan because a clear margin alone is not a cure.
The Whipple specimen includes the regional lymph nodes along the pancreatic head and hepatic artery.
Distal pancreatectomy removes the body and tail of the pancreas along with the spleen.
The spleen is removed with the pancreatic tail because its vessels run along the tumor and carry the draining lymph nodes.
The splenic artery and vein are divided and removed in a distal pancreatectomy for cancer.
A leak from the pancreatic stump is the characteristic complication of distal pancreatectomy.
About 28% of people develop new diabetes after distal pancreatectomy, most within a year or two.
Distal pancreatectomy is the counterpart of the Whipple for tumors of the body and tail and needs no rebuilt joins.
Staging laparoscopy is especially useful before distal pancreatectomy because body-and-tail tumors more often harbor hidden spread.
Whether a distal pancreatectomy is possible depends on the tumor’s relationship to the celiac artery at the base of the body.
The distal pancreatectomy specimen is examined for the posterior margin, splenic-vessel involvement and lymph nodes in the pathology report.
After splenectomy, fever is treated as an emergency because of the lifelong risk of overwhelming infection.
Distal pancreatectomy for cancer removes the lymph nodes along the splenic artery and at the splenic hilum.
Total pancreatectomy removes every part of the pancreas described in the overview, so all of its functions must be replaced.
Total pancreatectomy removes all islets, so insulin and glucagon production stop at once.
Total pancreatectomy removes all acinar cells, the enzyme-making cells, so no digestive enzymes are made and full replacement is required.
The universal insulin-dependent diabetes after total pancreatectomy is managed with insulin injections or a pump and glucose monitoring.
Digestion after total pancreatectomy depends entirely on enzyme replacement capsules with every meal and snack.
A planned Whipple is extended to a total pancreatectomy when the neck margin is positive or the tumor crosses the neck.
Total pancreatectomy combines the Whipple and the distal pancreatectomy in a single operation.
Total pancreatectomy removes the possibility of a pancreatic fistula but keeps the bleeding and bile-duct risks of a Whipple.
The type 3c diabetes after total pancreatectomy lacks glucagon as well as insulin, so low blood sugar is harder to correct.
Malnutrition affects about six in ten people a year after total pancreatectomy and needs dietitian follow-up.
A pancreas with precancerous cysts throughout its ducts is one reason a total pancreatectomy may be chosen.
The spleen is usually removed with the pancreatic tail during total pancreatectomy.
Vein resection removes and rebuilds a segment of the superior mesenteric or portal vein that the tumor touches.
Resection of the superior mesenteric artery is rarely attempted because its loss starves the bowel and causes intractable diarrhea.
Resection of the celiac or hepatic artery is a rare specialist operation because these arteries feed the liver.
The need for vein resection is predicted by the degree of tumor-vessel contact measured on CT.
Borderline resectable tumors are those whose vessel contact makes a vein resection likely; the term describes anatomy, not malignancy.
Vein resection is performed as part of a Whipple when a head tumor touches the superior mesenteric or portal vein.
Whether the tumor invaded the resected vein wall is reported by the pathologist and predicts outcome better than margin distance.
Chemotherapy before surgery is standard for tumors touching vessels, where converting a likely positive margin matters most.
After chemotherapy, scans often still show vessel contact that proves to be scar, so restaging does not by itself rule out vein resection.
Vein resection adds the risk of early clotting of the reconstructed vein to the usual complications of pancreatic surgery.
Body tumors reaching the celiac artery occasionally prompt arterial resection during distal pancreatectomy, a rare operation that none of the sources cited here studies.
The Whipple operation is where pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying and bleeding are most frequent, because it creates three new joins.
After distal pancreatectomy the fistula arises from the closed stump rather than from a join, graded by the same definitions.
Total pancreatectomy removes the possibility of a pancreatic fistula at the cost of lifelong diabetes.
Early complications shape the first weeks after a Whipple but did not reduce quality of life in five-year survivors.
Fever after pancreatic surgery is treated as a possible fistula, abscess or cholangitis until proven otherwise.
A pancreatic duct of 3 mm or less, together with a soft gland, defines the highest fistula risk after a Whipple.
Delayed gastric emptying after surgery causes nausea and vomiting until the stomach recovers its rhythm.
Fistula and delayed gastric emptying are managed partly with nutritional support while the gut heals.
The enzymes that leak in a pancreatic fistula are made by acinar cells, and they digest surrounding tissue.
A slow recovery from complications can delay or prevent chemotherapy after surgery, which affects the whole treatment plan.
When radiation is used, it usually follows months of induction chemotherapy rather than being the first treatment.
Chemoradiation is considered mainly in borderline resectable and locally advanced disease, where the question is local control or margin conversion.
Radiation improved local control without survival while Tumor Treating Fields improved survival without local control, in the same locally advanced setting.
Whether chemoradiation converted a margin is read by the pathologist on the resected specimen.
In the A021501 trial, SBRT added to mFOLFIRINOX did not improve margin-negative resection over mFOLFIRINOX alone.
The duodenum's tolerance limits the radiation dose that can be delivered to a tumor in the head of the pancreas.
SBRT improved pancreatic pain scores in the phase 2 trial that measured them.
Tumor Treating Fields were tested and approved only as an addition to gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel.
Tumor Treating Fields improved survival without local control, the mirror image of radiation's local control without survival.
The device is approved for locally advanced disease only, not for metastatic or resectable pancreatic cancer.
Tumor Treating Fields lengthened pain-free survival from 9.1 to 15.2 months in the pivotal trial.
The PANOVA-3 trial is an example of a trial that met its survival endpoint while missing its progression endpoint, which affects how its result should be read.
Tumors that have lost BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 function are the ones olaparib and other PARP inhibitors can kill.
ATM and other non-core repair genes do not predict PARP-inhibitor benefit the way biallelic BRCA loss does.
At least 16 weeks of platinum-containing chemotherapy, usually FOLFIRINOX, precedes maintenance olaparib.
The same repair defect that makes a tumor sensitive to olaparib makes it sensitive to oxaliplatin and other platinum drugs.
Eligibility for olaparib is established by a germline BRCA blood test, which cannot detect loss that arose only in the tumor.
A germline BRCA result that qualifies someone for olaparib also has implications for relatives, who may carry the same variant.
PARP inhibition exploits the loss of one DNA-repair pathway by blocking another.
Mismatch-repair-deficient pancreatic cancers are the only ones for which pembrolizumab is approved.
Eligibility for pembrolizumab depends on mismatch-repair or MSI testing, which can miss the defect in low-cellularity pancreatic specimens.
Checkpoint drugs combined with chemotherapy or vaccines have not improved survival in unselected pancreatic cancer.
Pembrolizumab works only where the tumor already displays antigens that T cells recognize, which mismatch-repair deficiency supplies.
Pembrolizumab releases the PD-1 brake on T cells so that those already recognizing the tumor stay active.
Mismatch-repair deficiency is several times more common in KRAS-wild-type pancreatic cancers than in KRAS-mutant ones.
Most mismatch-repair-deficient pancreatic cancers arise in people with Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition.
NRG1, RET and NTRK fusions and BRAF V600E are the rare targets for which fusion-directed drugs exist.
Fusions are found in 21 percent of KRAS-wild-type pancreatic cancers and essentially none of the KRAS-mutant ones.
Fusion-directed drugs can only be offered after RNA-based sequencing has found the fusion.
Drugs for FGFR2 and ALK fusions have no pancreatic approval and are reached through trials or off-label use.
A tumor driven by a fusion almost never also carries a KRAS mutation, because either alone drives the same pathway.
Daraxonrasib blocks the active form of mutant KRAS, the driver of most pancreatic cancers.
Daraxonrasib is the first multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor to reach approval, and the RASolute trials are its development program.
Most tumors eventually escape daraxonrasib through RAF, receptor or KRAS-copy changes or by routes not yet identified.
Daraxonrasib was tested and approved after at least one prior systemic therapy, the setting previously held by second-line chemotherapy.
The daraxonrasib label requires no RAS test, although the trial's endpoints were defined in RAS G12-mutant tumors.
RASolute 303 and 304 are testing daraxonrasib first-line and after surgery, with no results yet.
Resistance to daraxonrasib was read from circulating tumor DNA sequenced before treatment and at progression.
Escape from daraxonrasib reactivates the same pathway as escape from the earlier G12C-selective inhibitors, without binding-site mutations.
FOLFIRINOX is the pancreatic cancer regimen most often requiring growth-factor support, dose delays or dose reductions because of its high febrile-neutropenia risk.
Inherited slow-clearing UGT1A1 variants raise the febrile-neutropenia risk of irinotecan and are the reason for a lower starting dose in poor metabolizers.
Growth-factor support shortens the neutrophil trough during which fever and infection are most dangerous.
Irinotecan is the FOLFIRINOX component most often dose-reduced for neutropenia and the one whose clearance depends on UGT1A1.
Cachexia is hypothesized to force more dose reductions and delays, which is one rationale for the anti-cachexia drugs now in trials.

Oxaliplatin, whose dose-limiting toxicity is nerve damage rather than low blood counts, was stopped early by 55 percent of people on adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX, an adjustment growth factors cannot prevent.
A biliary stent relieves the jaundice and itching caused by a tumor compressing the bile duct.
The stent sits in the lower bile duct where it passes through the head of the pancreas and opens at the ampulla.
A stent placed before a Whipple operation is removed with the bile duct segment the operation takes out.
Months of chemotherapy before surgery are only feasible for a jaundiced person if a stent keeps the bile duct open throughout.
A blocked biliary stent produces the same returning jaundice and cholangitis risk as the original obstruction.
A biliary stent is a route for bacteria into the bloodstream, so fever in a stented person raises the question of cholangitis.
Enzyme replacement therapy is the treatment for the exocrine insufficiency that a pancreatic tumor or resection causes.
Enzyme capsules replace the lipase, protease and amylase that acinar cells can no longer deliver to the intestine.
After a Whipple operation, enzyme replacement raises fat absorption but normalizes it in only about a quarter of people because the rebuilt anatomy mistimes enzyme release.
Loss of the duodenum removes the bicarbonate-rich chamber where enzymes and food normally mix, which limits how well enzyme capsules work.
Enzyme replacement corrects the digestive share of weight loss but not the cachexia driven by inflammatory signals (cytokines) that acts independently of digestion.
Enzyme capsules are the precondition for dietary advice to work, since food that is not digested cannot be absorbed.
Enzyme capsules with every meal and snack are a routine part of eating after a Whipple or pancreatectomy.
Blood sugar after surgery depends on whether a person's pre-existing diabetes was paraneoplastic, which can resolve, or long-standing, which persists.
Diabetes after surgery follows from loss of islets, and its timing depends on how much islet capacity the remnant retains.
Total pancreatectomy causes immediate, lifelong insulin-dependent diabetes in every patient because no islets remain.
After distal pancreatectomy, 28 percent of people developed new diabetes at a median of about a year in a national cohort.
After a Whipple, new diabetes developed in 24 to 30 percent of people in cohorts followed for six months to three years.
Glucose monitoring belongs in long-term follow-up after a Whipple because surgical diabetes can appear years later.
The dexamethasone given with chemotherapy to prevent nausea raises blood sugar transiently after each infusion.
Anticoagulants are both the preventive option and the treatment for the clots that pancreatic cancer causes.
About a third of clots in pancreatic cancer form in the portal, splenic or mesenteric veins rather than the legs or lungs.
Clot risk is highest in the months after chemotherapy starts, which is when prevention trials enrolled people; in the French cohort most were on platinum- or gemcitabine-based regimens.
Endoscopic procedures such as stent exchange are a common reason anticoagulants are paused, during which clot risk returns.
Bleeding after surgery and clot prevention around surgery pull in opposite directions and are balanced by the surgical team.
Tumors in the neck (isthmus) of the pancreas carried about twice the clot risk of other locations in the French cohort.
The drugs and nutritional measures described here are the treatments being used or tested for the cachexia that pancreatic cancer causes.
Dietary counseling and protein supplements are the foundation on which any cachexia drug would be added.
Ponsegromab's phase 3 trial is the main cachexia study now recruiting in pancreatic cancer.
Cachexia treatments address the signal-driven loss of muscle, whereas enzyme replacement addresses the digestive loss of calories; both are usually needed.
Resistance training improved strength but not CT-measured muscle in pancreatic cancer, which is why drugs targeting the catabolic signal are being tested.
If cachexia forces dose reductions and delays, reversing it could change how much chemotherapy is delivered, a hypothesis the phase 3 trial can test.
Anamorelin raised blood sugar or caused new diabetes in about 6 percent of people each, a concern in a disease already linked to diabetes.
KRAS G12C inhibitors lock one specific mutant form of the KRAS protein in its switched-off state.
KRAS G12C is one of the rarer alleles in pancreatic cancer, at about 1 to 3 percent of cases, compared with G12D at roughly four in ten.
Eligibility for a KRAS G12C inhibitor is established by sequencing tumor tissue or circulating tumor DNA for the G12C allele.
Tumors escape KRAS G12C inhibitors by reactivating the same pathway through new KRAS copies, receptor signaling or RAF changes.
Elironrasib applies the RAS(ON) design to KRAS G12C and is being tested after first-generation G12C inhibitors stop working.
Daraxonrasib, the approved RAS inhibitor, covers KRAS G12C together with the other RAS mutations rather than one allele.
KRAS G12D inhibitors act on the most common mutant form of the KRAS protein in pancreatic cancer.
KRAS G12D accounts for roughly four in ten pancreatic cancers, so a G12D-selective drug would reach far more patients than a G12C drug.
In mice, blocking KRAS G12D draws T cells into the tumor, and those T cells are needed to keep the tumor from regrowing.
Zoldonrasib is being tested together with daraxonrasib, which covers KRAS G12D along with the other RAS mutations.
Zoldonrasib belongs to the RAS(ON) tri-complex family that also produced daraxonrasib.
The short immune window after KRAS G12D inhibition in mice is the rationale for testing immunotherapy early in RAS-directed treatment.
RASolute 305 and RASolute 309 are the phase 3 trials of zoldonrasib in metastatic pancreatic cancer, both recruiting.
Daraxonrasib is the approved member of the multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor class, and its own entry carries the trial detail.
Multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitors block the ON state of mutant and normal KRAS, NRAS and HRAS.
Elironrasib applies the RAS(ON) design to KRAS G12C alone and is being tested after first-generation G12C inhibitors fail.
Zoldonrasib applies the RAS(ON) tri-complex design to KRAS G12D and is being tested alone and with daraxonrasib.
RAS(ON) inhibition regressed mouse tumors where SHP2 and MEK inhibitors, the pathway drugs that failed in earlier trials, did not.
Tumors escape RAS(ON) inhibitors mostly without a detectable genetic cause, and never through drug-binding-site mutations in pancreatic cohorts.
RASolute 304 tests whether daraxonrasib after surgery and chemotherapy delays recurrence from microscopic disease that scans cannot see.
The RASolute 302 trial was open-label and its full publication is available only as an abstract, so its numbers come from the abstract and the FDA approval page.
Resistance to RAS inhibitors is what eventually ends the benefit most people get from daraxonrasib.
Multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitors are the class in which the daraxonrasib resistance patterns described here were measured.
KRAS G12C inhibitors supplied the first human resistance data, including the drug-binding-site mutations that pancreatic cohorts do not show.
A shift between classical and basal-like cell states is one of the non-genetic routes by which pancreatic cancer survives RAS blockade.
Resistance to RAS inhibitors is mostly measured by sequencing circulating tumor DNA before treatment and again at progression.
The combination strategies aimed at resistance are tested against the record of earlier attempts on the KRAS pathway, which failed in people.
Every strategy described here attacked a protein beside KRAS because KRAS itself could not be bound by a drug.
Daraxonrasib was the first drug aimed at this pathway to produce a large randomized survival benefit in pancreatic cancer, after the failures described here.
The adaptive reactivation that defeated MEK and EGFR inhibitors is the same process that now underlies resistance to RAS inhibitors.
The erlotinib trial shows why a significant hazard ratio and a ten-day median gain can describe the same result.
This run of negative pathway trials is the historical background against which any new pancreatic cancer result is judged.
A personalized mRNA vaccine works by loading antigen-presenting cells with mutant protein fragments, the step pancreatic cancer otherwise performs poorly.
The mRNA vaccine's measurable product is new cytotoxic T-cell clones in the blood, which persisted for more than two years in most vaccinated patients.
Personalized mRNA vaccines are built from each patient's private mutations, whereas KRAS vaccines target a mutation shared across most pancreatic cancers.
Vaccines after surgery are aimed at microscopic disease that imaging cannot see, which is why the trials measure recurrence rather than tumor shrinkage.
Circulating tumor DNA at the time of vaccination is the measurement that would separate a true vaccine effect from a responder group that simply had less cancer left.
The responder-versus-non-responder comparison in the mRNA vaccine trial is a worked example of why a within-arm split is not a treatment effect.
Autogene cevumeran is available only inside a clinical trial, and its randomized test is closed to new enrollment with results expected around 2031.
KRAS vaccines target the mutant KRAS protein itself, which is why a mutation present in the great majority of pancreatic cancers can serve as one shared vaccine target.
A shared-antigen KRAS vaccine only fits patients whose tumor carries one of the covered variants, so KRAS-wild-type pancreatic cancers fall outside these trials.
ELI-002 is engineered to accumulate in the draining lymph nodes, because that is where T cells are primed against a new antigen.
The KRAS vaccine trials select and follow patients by circulating tumor DNA and serum markers, because by design the participants have no tumor visible on imaging.
Shared-antigen KRAS vaccines and personalized mRNA vaccines share the same unresolved question: an immune response has been shown, a survival benefit has not.
Both the KRAS peptide vaccine and the GVAX whole-cell vaccine act by supplying antigen-presenting cells with material, a step this cancer performs poorly on its own.
The two different hazard ratios reported from the same 25-patient KRAS vaccine trial illustrate how much a data-derived threshold can change an apparent result.
Engineered T-cell therapy replaces the T cell's own target recognition with a transferred receptor, bypassing the need for the patient's immune system to find the tumor by itself.
A transferred T-cell receptor still depends on the tumor displaying its target through HLA, whereas a chimeric antigen receptor does not, which is why the two designs fail in different ways.
Mutant KRAS is the target of the receptor-engineered cells that produced the one dramatic pancreatic response, which required the patient to carry the HLA-C*08:02 tissue type as well.
Eligibility for KRAS-directed cell therapy depends on testing both the tumor's KRAS variant and the patient's HLA type, since the therapy only works when both match.
Lymph-node-targeted vaccination, the delivery idea behind the KRAS peptide vaccines, eradicated established mouse tumors when used to re-stimulate transferred receptor-engineered T cells.
No engineered T-cell product is approved for pancreatic cancer, so the published pancreatic experience comes from phase 1 trials and single-patient authorizations.
CXCR4, CCR2 and CSF1R blockers were designed to strip suppressive macrophages and monocytes out of the pancreatic tumor, and in patients they measurably did so.
Immune combinations raise the number of CD8 T cells inside pancreatic tumors, and in the same specimens they raise regulatory T cells that restrain them.
Pembrolizumab in mismatch-repair-deficient tumors is the one approved immune route in pancreatic cancer, and it is the exception these unselected combination trials run into.
Mismatch repair deficiency, present in under 1 percent of pancreatic cancers, is the molecular feature that separates the patients checkpoint blockade helps from the great majority it does not.
Immune combinations and stroma-directed drugs repeat the same pattern: a target is measurably engaged in the tumor and survival does not change.
The CXCR4 combination's fall from a 32 percent interim response rate to 18.6 percent at full accrual is a worked example of why interim numbers are not conclusions.
Cachexia research targets the biology behind the weight and muscle loss that this symptom entry describes from the patient's side.
The investigational agents here sit alongside the appetite and nutrition measures currently available, none of which reverses muscle loss.
A blinded trial of 18 grams of daily protein after pancreatic resection improved walking speed and quality of life, which is why dietitian involvement is standard rather than optional.
Exercise during preoperative treatment improved walking distance in 50 patients, and in resected specimens was associated with denser tumor blood vessels and more CD8 T cells.
Exercise acts through an interleukin-15 pathway that mobilizes CD8 T cells into pancreatic tumors in mice, with more CD8 cells seen in tumors from patients who exercised.
Anamorelin raises blood sugar and caused new diabetes in about 6 percent of trial patients, which matters in a disease where diabetes is already common.
Reprogramming strategies act on the fibroblast states this entry describes, pushing suppressive ones toward rest rather than clearing the whole population.
Reprogramming treats desmoplasia (the dense scar around the tumor) as a composition problem rather than as excess tissue to be dissolved, because clearing it wholesale shortened survival in mice.
The failures of hedgehog inhibition and bulk fibroblast depletion are the lessons that reprogramming and subtype-selective depletion were designed around.
Losartan was added to neoadjuvant chemotherapy on the premise that reducing matrix and tissue pressure improves drug delivery, a premise the trial did not measure.
LRRC15-positive myofibroblasts directly suppress CD8 T-cell function in mice, and removing them improved the response to checkpoint blockade.
Returning stellate cells toward quiescence raised vessel patency and intratumoral chemotherapy levels in mice, whereas depleting myofibroblasts markedly increased hypoxia.
Subtype-selective fibroblast depletion improved anti-PD-L1 response in mice, which is the preclinical rationale behind pairing stroma-directed and immune drugs.
Judging whether a result counts as progress starts with reading its endpoints, which is what the topic on treatment results sets out.
A trial's phase and registry status describe where it stands, while this topic asks whether its result changes anything.
Daraxonrasib is the pancreatic cancer result in which response, progression-free survival and overall survival moved together in a randomized trial.
Immune combination trials supply most of the pancreatic examples of early results that shrank toward nothing under randomization.
The personalized mRNA vaccine is a phase 1 result whose randomized test has no posted outcomes, which is why it is not yet progress.
The stroma-directed trials are the clearest pancreatic examples of tumor response rising while survival does not.
